entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Having the opposite effect to the one you wanted, so that an action makes a problem worse instead of better.
entries.usage: Common at work, in parenting and in news about policy, and fine in both speech and writing. It usually comes after a verb: *be*, *prove*, *turn out to be*, and very often *can be* or *would be* as a polite warning. The pattern *it's counterproductive to* + verb is typical.
entries.pattern: be / prove / turn out (to be) counterproductive; it's counterproductive to + verb
examples: Yelling at a toddler who is already upset is almost always **counterproductive**.
Skipping breakfast to lose weight can be **counterproductive** if you end up snacking all afternoon.
Cutting the customer service team to save money turned out to be **counterproductive**: complaints doubled within a month.

drill.sentence: Raising ticket prices was {{counterproductive}}: so many fans stayed home that the stadium made less money than before.
drill.hint: had the opposite effect to what was intended (not *self-defeating*)

mistake.wrong: Working through the night would be contraproductive.
mistake.right: Working through the night would be counterproductive.
mistake.why: English uses the prefix *counter-*; *contra-* comes from German *kontraproduktiv*.

entries.related: *self-defeating* — similar, stresses that it destroys its own goal; *backfire* — the verb for the same result (*the plan backfired*); *constructive* — the opposite, helpful.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make someone feel that they don't belong or are no longer welcome, so that they become unfriendly or stop supporting you.
entries.usage: Common in talk about families, friends, teams, customers and fans: *alienate customers*, *alienate your coworkers*. It often appears with *risk* (*risk alienating*) as a warning. The adjective *alienated* (feeling cut off from a group or society) is just as common; in casual speech people also say *push someone away*.
entries.pattern: alienate + customers / fans / friends / coworkers; alienate someone from a group
examples: If you keep criticizing her boyfriend, you'll only **alienate** your daughter.
The diner **alienated** its regulars when it doubled the prices and dropped half the menu.
His constant jokes about her accent slowly **alienated** her from the rest of the team.

drill.sentence: The band risked {{alienating}} its oldest fans, who felt the new dance songs weren't made for them anymore.
drill.hint: making people feel they no longer belong (not *losing* or *disappointing*)

entries.related: *estranged* — usually of family members who no longer speak (*estranged from her father*); *push away* — informal; *win over* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The one point in a process where things slow down or get stuck, which limits the speed of the whole process; also a narrow part of a road where traffic slows.
entries.usage: Very common at work, in engineering, logistics and traffic reports, in both speech and writing. Typical phrases: *the main bottleneck*, *a bottleneck in* + process, *create*, *remove* or *ease a bottleneck*. It describes a structural problem, not just a single delay.
entries.pattern: the (main / real) bottleneck in + process; create / remove / ease a bottleneck
examples: Approvals were the real **bottleneck**: every request sat on one manager's desk for a week.
Traffic backs up every morning at the **bottleneck** where the highway narrows to one lane.
On busy nights the kitchen is the **bottleneck**; there are free tables, but the cooks can't keep up.

drill.sentence: At the airport, security was the {{bottleneck}}: check-in took five minutes, but the line for the scanners took an hour.
drill.hint: the narrow point that slowed everything down (not *holdup* or *problem*)

entries.related: *holdup* — informal, any delay; *choke point* — a narrow place that is easy to block; *backlog* — work that has piled up, often because of a bottleneck.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Too full of things in an untidy way, so that a space is hard to use or to look at.
entries.usage: Used for rooms, desks, closets and garages, and also for screens, web pages and slides (*a cluttered layout*). The pattern is *cluttered with* + things. The noun *clutter* (uncountable) and the verb *declutter* are very common in American talk about homes; *messy* is more general and can also mean dirty.
entries.pattern: a cluttered + room / desk / closet / screen; cluttered with + things
examples: My desk is so **cluttered** with mail and coffee mugs that I can't find my keys.
The website looks **cluttered**; there are ads in every corner of the page.
After the kids moved out, the garage stayed **cluttered** with old bikes and boxes for years.

drill.sentence: The hall closet was so {{cluttered}} that a pile of shoes fell out every time we opened the door.
drill.hint: untidy and too full of objects (not *messy*, *packed*, *stuffed* or *crammed*)

entries.related: *messy* — untidy or dirty, more general; *crowded* — too full of people; *tidy* or *clutter-free* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person, thing or value that is very different from all the others in a group.
entries.usage: Originally a statistics term for a data point far from the rest, it is now common in news, sports and everyday talk (*That year was an outlier*). It is neutral: an outlier can be unusually good, bad or just different. Typical phrases: *a bit of an outlier*, *an outlier among* + group, *remove the outliers*.
entries.pattern: an outlier (among / in + group); remove / exclude outliers
examples: One house on our street sold for twice the asking price, but that was an **outlier**.
With six kids, we were an **outlier** on a street full of retired couples.
Once we removed the **outliers**, the average delivery time dropped from nine days to two.

drill.sentence: Almost everyone on the trip loved the spicy food; Sam, who only ate plain rice, was the {{outlier}}.
drill.hint: the one very different from the rest of the group (not *exception*)

entries.related: *exception* — a case that a rule doesn't cover; *anomaly* — something unexpected, more formal; *the norm* — the opposite, what is typical.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The difference between two amounts, especially the number of votes, points or seconds by which someone wins; in business, the difference between cost and selling price (profit margin).
entries.usage: Common in sports, election and business news: *win by a wide*, *narrow* or *slim margin*, *by a margin of* + number. In business, the plural *margins* usually means profit margins: *thin margins*, *high-margin products*. *Margin of error* is the possible error in a poll or measurement.
entries.pattern: win by a narrow / wide margin; a (profit) margin of 20 percent; thin / tight margins
examples: The home team won by a narrow **margin** after scoring in the last minute.
Grocery stores work on very thin **margins**, often just two or three cents on every dollar.
The **margin** between first and second place was less than a tenth of a second.

drill.sentence: We sell the lamps for $80 and they cost us $50 to make, so our {{margin}} is almost 40 percent.
drill.hint: the share of the price that is profit (not *profit* or *markup*)

entries.related: *lead* — how far ahead someone is during a contest; *markup* — the amount added to the cost price; *margin of error* — the possible error in a poll or measurement.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A new business or project, especially one with a real risk of losing money.
entries.usage: Common in business news and in conversation about careers: *a business venture*, *a new venture*, *a joint venture* (two companies working together), *venture capital* (money invested in young companies). For a small project it can sound grand, so people sometimes use it with a smile (*my latest venture*).
entries.pattern: a (new / business / joint) venture; venture capital
examples: After twenty years as a nurse, she put her savings into her first business **venture**, a small bakery.
The two carmakers formed a joint **venture** to build batteries in Ohio.
His last **venture**, a food truck selling fancy grilled cheese, closed after six months.

drill.sentence: Opening a restaurant is a risky {{venture}}; most new places close within a few years.
drill.hint: a new business project with a chance of losing money (not *business*, *project* or *investment*)

entries.related: *startup* — a young company, usually in tech; *enterprise* — a business, or a bold project, more formal; *undertaking* — any large task.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A group of people, organizations or political parties that join together to reach a shared goal, often for a limited time.
entries.usage: Common in news: *a coalition of* + groups, *form*, *build* or *join a coalition*, *a coalition government* (normal in parliamentary countries, rare in the US). Americans use it a lot for local alliances (*a coalition of parents and teachers*). It suggests separate groups that keep their own identity.
entries.pattern: a coalition of + groups; form / build / join a coalition; a coalition government
examples: A **coalition** of parents, teachers and local businesses raised money to keep the library open on weekends.
After the election, no party had a majority, so three of them formed a **coalition** government.
The **coalition** fell apart when two of the groups disagreed about how to spend the money.

drill.sentence: Twenty neighborhood groups joined a {{coalition}} to fight the plan for a new highway through the park.
drill.hint: an organized group of separate groups with a shared goal (not *alliance* or *network*)

entries.related: *alliance* — similar, often long-term or between countries; *partnership* — usually two parties; *faction* — a group inside a larger group, often in conflict with it.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To refuse to accept or give in to something, such as a change, pressure or a temptation.
entries.usage: Typical objects: *resist change*, *resist pressure*, *resist arrest*, *resist the temptation / urge to* + verb. *I couldn't resist* (with a noun, an *-ing* form or nothing) is a very common, light way to admit you gave in to something nice. *Resist* takes a noun or an *-ing* form, not a *to*-infinitive.
entries.pattern: resist + change / pressure / arrest; resist the temptation / urge to + verb; can't resist + noun / -ing
examples: Many longtime employees **resisted** the move to an open-plan office.
Try to **resist** the urge to check your phone during dinner.
The suspect **resisted** arrest and had to be held down by two officers.

drill.sentence: I'm supposed to be cutting back on sugar, but I couldn't {{resist}} a slice of my sister's chocolate cake.
drill.hint: stop myself from taking something tempting (not *refuse* or *skip*)

mistake.wrong: I couldn't resist to buy another pair of sneakers.
mistake.right: I couldn't resist buying another pair of sneakers.
mistake.why: *Resist* takes a noun or an *-ing* form; the *to*-infinitive comes only after *the temptation* or *the urge*.

entries.related: *oppose* — be against, often openly; *withstand* — not be damaged by force or pressure; *give in (to)* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The largest or main part of something, used in the phrase *the bulk of*.
entries.usage: Almost always *the bulk of* + noun: *the bulk of the work*, *the bulk of our customers*. It is common in speech, news and business writing and a little more formal than *most of*. The verb usually agrees with the noun after *of* (*the bulk of the money goes*, *the bulk of the students are*); *buy in bulk* is a different sense, meaning in large quantities.
entries.pattern: the bulk of + noun
examples: The **bulk** of the cleanup was done by volunteers who showed up on Saturday morning.
Rent eats up the **bulk** of my paycheck every month.
The **bulk** of the rain is expected overnight, so the morning commute should be dry.

drill.sentence: My brother did the {{bulk}} of the driving on our road trip, so I mostly picked the music.
drill.hint: the largest part (not *majority* or *lion's share*)

entries.related: *most of* — plainer; *the majority of* — usually with plural nouns (*the majority of voters*); *in bulk* — in large quantities (*buy rice in bulk*).

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The official power to make legal decisions and enforce laws, or the area or type of case where this power applies.
entries.usage: Common in legal and news language: *have* or *lack jurisdiction over*, *fall under the jurisdiction of*, *outside our jurisdiction*. It matters a lot in the US, where federal, state, county and city authorities each have their own. In everyday talk it is also used jokingly for someone's area of responsibility (*That's not my jurisdiction*).
entries.pattern: have / lack jurisdiction over + area / case; fall under / outside the jurisdiction of
examples: The crash happened just outside city limits, so it was under the sheriff's **jurisdiction**.
The judge said her court had no **jurisdiction** over the dispute, so the case was dismissed.
Don't ask me about the kids' bedtime; that's their dad's **jurisdiction**.

drill.sentence: The building is on federal land, so the state inspectors have no {{jurisdiction}} over it.
drill.hint: the official right to make legal decisions there (not *authority* or *power*)

entries.related: *authority* — power to give orders or decide, more general; *purview* — the range of things a person or body deals with, formal; *domain* — an area of responsibility or knowledge.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Similar enough in size, quality or type that it makes sense to compare them; roughly equal.
entries.usage: Common in business, news and shopping talk: *comparable to* or *with* + noun, *comparable in price / size / quality*, *a comparable salary*. Careful speakers stress the first syllable (KAHM-per-uh-bul), although kum-PAIR-uh-bul is also common. American real estate agents call similar nearby homes *comps*, short for *comparables*.
entries.pattern: comparable to / with + noun; comparable in + size / price / quality
examples: She found a job with a **comparable** salary and a much shorter commute.
The two phones are **comparable** in price, but one has a far better camera.
In the trial, the new drug's side effects were **comparable** to those of a placebo.

drill.sentence: We looked at three houses of {{comparable}} size in the area, and they all cost about $400,000.
drill.hint: roughly the same, so it's fair to put them side by side (not *similar*, *equal* or *equivalent*)

entries.related: *similar* — alike in some way; *equivalent* — equal in value or function; *incomparable* — so good that nothing else is close.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An area of activity, interest or knowledge, or the kind of thing something belongs to.
entries.usage: Neutral to slightly formal, and very common in fixed phrases: *within* or *beyond the realm of possibility*, *in the realm of* + field, *outside my realm of expertise*. The old meaning, a kingdom, now sounds literary or belongs to fantasy stories. It has one syllable and rhymes with *helm*.
entries.pattern: in / within / beyond the realm of + noun; the realm of possibility
examples: Questions about taxes are outside my **realm** of expertise, so you should ask an accountant.
Flying cars still belong to the **realm** of science fiction.
In the **realm** of youth sports, the parents are often more competitive than the kids.

drill.sentence: Winning the lottery is technically within the {{realm}} of possibility, but I wouldn't count on it.
drill.hint: area (fixed phrase with *of possibility*; not *bounds* or *range*)

entries.related: *field* — an area of study or work, plainer; *sphere* — an area of activity or influence (*the public sphere*); *domain* — an area of knowledge or control.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The official decision of a jury or judge about whether someone is guilty; also any final opinion about something after trying or thinking about it.
entries.usage: In court: *reach*, *return* or *deliver a verdict*, *a guilty / not-guilty verdict*. In everyday talk it is a light, slightly playful word for an opinion: *So, what's the verdict?* after someone tries food, a movie or a new haircut. In a US jury trial the jury gives the verdict; the judge then gives the *sentence*.
entries.pattern: reach / return / deliver a verdict; a guilty / not-guilty verdict; What's the verdict?
examples: After two days of discussion, the jury returned a **verdict** of not guilty.
You've tried both pizzas, so what's the **verdict**?
The early **verdict** from fans is that the new stadium is great but the parking is a nightmare.

drill.sentence: The jury took less than an hour to reach a {{verdict}}, and the defendant was found guilty on all counts.
drill.hint: the jury's official finding of guilty or not guilty (not *decision*)

mistake.wrong: The judge gave him a verdict of ten years in prison.
mistake.right: The judge gave him a sentence of ten years in prison.
mistake.why: The *verdict* is guilty or not guilty; the punishment is the *sentence* (German *Urteil* covers both).

entries.related: *sentence* — the punishment a judge gives after a guilty verdict; *ruling* — a judge's decision on a legal question; *judgment* — a court's decision, or any opinion.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Completely or totally; it makes a strong word even stronger.
entries.usage: It mostly combines with negative or extreme words: *utterly exhausted*, *utterly ridiculous*, *utterly confused*, *utterly failed*. It sounds stronger and a little more emotional than *completely*. With positive words (*utterly charming*) it is possible but sounds a bit literary.
entries.pattern: utterly + exhausted / ridiculous / confused / unacceptable / destroyed
examples: By the end of the move, we were **utterly** exhausted and fell asleep on a mattress on the floor.
The movie was **utterly** forgettable; a week later I couldn't tell you a single scene.
I was **utterly** confused by the tax form until a friend explained it to me.

drill.sentence: After the hurricane, the little beach town was {{utterly}} destroyed; hardly a house was left standing.
drill.hint: a strong intensifier for extreme words (not *completely*, *totally*, *entirely* or *absolutely*)

entries.related: *completely* — the neutral word; *totally* — more casual; *absolutely* — common with extreme adjectives, positive or negative (*absolutely furious*, *absolutely amazing*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Surprising in a way that teaches you something new or shows you the truth about a situation.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, reviews and personal stories: *an eye-opening experience / trip / book / documentary*, *It was really eye-opening*. It is usually positive about the learning, even when what you learned was unpleasant. The noun is *an eye-opener*: *That trip was a real eye-opener*.
entries.pattern: an eye-opening + experience / trip / book; It was (really) eye-opening.
examples: Spending a day with an ER nurse was really **eye-opening**; she barely sat down in twelve hours.
Tracking my spending for a month was **eye-opening**: I'd spent $200 on takeout alone.
The documentary gives an **eye-opening** look at what happens to the clothes we throw away.

drill.sentence: My first trip outside the US was {{eye-opening}}: I realized how differently people live in other places.
drill.hint: surprising, and it taught me a lot (not *enlightening*, *revealing* or *life-changing*)

entries.related: *an eye-opener* — the noun; *enlightening* — teaches you a lot, a bit more formal; *revealing* — shows something that was hidden.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Lasting or holding a job only for a short time, until a permanent person or arrangement is in place.
entries.usage: Common in news and organizations, and always before a noun: *an interim CEO / director / principal*, *an interim report*, *an interim solution*. The phrase *in the interim* means *in the meantime* and sounds formal. The stress is on the first syllable.
entries.pattern: interim + CEO / director / report / solution; in the interim
examples: After the principal retired suddenly, the vice principal served as **interim** principal until June.
As an **interim** solution, we're using paper tickets until the new system is ready.
We'll know more in a few weeks. In the **interim**, please keep all your receipts.

drill.sentence: The board named the finance director {{interim}} CEO while it searched for a permanent replacement.
drill.hint: filling the role only for a short time (not *acting* or *temporary*)

entries.related: *acting* — doing a job temporarily, often for someone who is away (*acting manager*); *temporary* — plainer, for anything; *permanent* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Playing an important part in making something happen.
entries.usage: Used after *be* or in *play an instrumental role in*, followed by a noun or an *-ing* form. Common in praise, thank-you emails, speeches and news: *She was instrumental in getting the project approved*. It usually describes people, sometimes things (*Online reviews were instrumental in…*).
entries.pattern: be instrumental in + noun / -ing; play an instrumental role in
examples: Our neighbor was **instrumental** in getting speed bumps installed on our street.
Thanks for everything, Raj; you were **instrumental** in making this launch happen.
Volunteers played an **instrumental** role in rebuilding the town after the flood.

drill.sentence: My high school chemistry teacher was {{instrumental}} in my decision to study medicine.
drill.hint: played a key part (not *key*, *important* or *influential*)

mistake.wrong: He was instrumental to save the company.
mistake.right: He was instrumental in saving the company.
mistake.why: After *instrumental in*, use a noun or an *-ing* form, not a *to*-infinitive.

entries.related: *key* — plainer (*a key role*); *pivotal* — central to the result, more formal; *play a big part in* — the everyday phrase.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Complete and not damaged, especially after something that could have harmed it.
entries.usage: Usually after a verb: *be*, *remain*, *stay*, *survive* or *arrive intact*, *keep something intact*. It works for objects and buildings and also for abstract things such as a reputation, a family or a sense of humor. It is neutral and common in news and everyday speech.
entries.pattern: remain / stay / survive / arrive intact; keep something intact
examples: The box fell down the stairs, but somehow every glass inside was still **intact**.
The old church survived the earthquake almost **intact**.
After the scandal, her reputation remained surprisingly **intact**.

drill.sentence: We shipped my mom's old vase across the country in bubble wrap, and it arrived {{intact}}.
drill.hint: with nothing broken (adjective; not *undamaged*, *unbroken* or *in one piece*)

entries.related: *undamaged* — plainer, physical only; *in one piece* — informal, also for people (*She got home in one piece*); *unscathed* — not hurt at all.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A permanent job as a professor or teacher, which protects you from being fired without serious cause; also the period of time someone holds a job or office.
entries.usage: In US universities tenure is a central career goal: *get*, *be granted* or *be denied tenure*, *a tenure-track job* (one that can lead to tenure), *a tenured professor*. Many public school teachers can also earn it. The second sense is common in news everywhere: *during her tenure as CEO*.
entries.pattern: get / be granted / be denied tenure; a tenure-track job; during someone's tenure as + role
examples: She finally got **tenure** after seven years of teaching and writing two books.
During his **tenure** as mayor, the city built three new parks.
In many states, public school teachers can earn **tenure** after a few years in the classroom.

drill.sentence: He was denied {{tenure}} last spring, so he has one more year at the university before he has to find a new job.
drill.hint: a permanent post as a professor (not *a promotion* or *a contract*)

entries.related: *tenure-track* — a job that can lead to tenure; *tenured* — the adjective (*a tenured professor*); *term* — a fixed period in office, as for a mayor or senator.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To get involved in someone else's situation or decisions when they don't want you to.
entries.usage: It sounds critical: *Stop interfering!*, *interfere in* someone's life, marriage or plans. *Interfere with* + thing means stop it from working properly (*Caffeine interferes with sleep*). A person who does this a lot is *interfering* (*an interfering relative*); *I don't want to interfere, but…* is a polite way to give unwanted advice.
entries.pattern: interfere in + someone's life / affairs / plans; interfere with + something (stop it working)
examples: My mother-in-law means well, but she **interferes** in everything, even how we fold the towels.
I don't want to **interfere**, but are you sure that guy is good for you?
Officials denied that the company had **interfered** in the investigation.

drill.sentence: I know you're trying to help, but please stop {{interfering}} in our wedding plans; we can handle it.
drill.hint: pushing into matters that aren't yours (not *meddling*)

entries.related: *meddle* — similar, even more critical; *butt in* — informal, interrupt or get involved rudely; *stay out of it* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Serious discussion and communication about a subject, especially the way a topic is discussed in public or in a particular field.
entries.usage: Formal and uncountable in this sense, common in academic writing, journalism and opinion pieces: *public discourse*, *political discourse*, *civil discourse*, *the discourse around* + topic. Online, *the discourse* is also used half-ironically for endless arguments on social media. For a single conversation, say *discussion*, not *a discourse*.
entries.pattern: public / political / civil / academic discourse; the discourse around / on + topic
examples: Many people feel that public **discourse** has become angrier since social media took over.
In academic **discourse**, the word “significant” usually has a statistical meaning.
The **discourse** around remote work has changed a lot since 2020.

drill.sentence: Name-calling and personal insults have no place in civil {{discourse}}.
drill.hint: formal word for serious public communication (not *debate*, *dialogue*, *discussion* or *society*)

entries.related: *discussion* — the everyday word; *debate* — an argument between sides; *rhetoric* — language meant to persuade, often used critically.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A medicine or treatment for an illness, especially a simple or traditional one; also a way of solving a problem.
entries.usage: In health: *a home remedy*, *a natural / herbal remedy*, *a remedy for* + illness. For problems it sounds a little formal: *a remedy for* the housing shortage, and the verb *remedy the situation*. The normal preposition is *for*; a *remedy* helps, while a *cure* ends the illness completely.
entries.pattern: a (home / natural) remedy for + illness / problem; remedy the situation (verb)
examples: Doctors say there's no proven **remedy** for the common cold; rest is still the best advice.
There's no quick **remedy** for a housing shortage; it takes years to build enough homes.
Honestly, the only **remedy** for a bad haircut is time.

drill.sentence: Ginger tea is my mom's favorite home {{remedy}} for an upset stomach.
drill.hint: a simple traditional way to treat an illness (not *cure*)

entries.related: *cure* — something that ends an illness completely; *treatment* — medical care in general; *solution* — the plain word for fixing a problem.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: As a group, with everyone or everything taken together rather than separately.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and formal speech: *collectively own*, *collectively responsible*, *(be) known collectively as* + a group name. It stresses the group as a whole, often with numbers or responsibility. In casual speech, *together* or *as a group* is more natural.
entries.pattern: collectively + own / decide / responsible; (be) known collectively as
examples: The five roommates **collectively** spend over $300 a month on streaming services.
Fixing the playground isn't one person's job; we're **collectively** responsible as a neighborhood.
Lettuce, spinach and kale are known **collectively** as leafy greens.

drill.sentence: The three sisters {{collectively}} own the family farm, so no one can sell it without the others.
drill.hint: as a group rather than separately (not *jointly*, *together* or *equally*)

entries.related: *jointly* — shared by two or more, often legal (*jointly owned*); *individually* — the opposite; *as a whole* — taken all together.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Existing in large quantities; more than enough.
entries.usage: Neutral to slightly formal, common in writing about nature, food and resources: *abundant wildlife*, *abundant rainfall*, *abundant evidence*. In everyday speech, *plenty of* or *lots of* is more natural. The noun is *abundance*, often in *in abundance* (*Fruit grows here in abundance*).
entries.pattern: abundant + wildlife / rainfall / evidence / resources; in abundance
examples: Fresh peaches are **abundant** at the farmers market in August, and they're cheap.
The park has **abundant** wildlife, so keep your food locked in the car at night.
Despite **abundant** evidence that sleep matters, most of us still don't get enough.

drill.sentence: Fish are so {{abundant}} in this lake that even beginners usually catch something.
drill.hint: present in large numbers (not *plentiful*, *common* or *numerous*)

entries.related: *plentiful* — very similar; *ample* — enough or more than enough (*ample time*); *scarce* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To be extremely good at something, or much better than most people at it.
entries.usage: Slightly formal; common in school reports, job ads, reference letters and sports writing. *Excel at* is usual for skills and activities (*excel at languages*, *excel at solving problems*), *excel in* for subjects and fields (*excel in math*). In casual speech people more often say *be really good at*.
entries.pattern: excel at + activity / -ing; excel in + subject / field
examples: She's always **excelled** at languages; she spoke four by the time she was sixteen.
Our son is quiet in class but **excels** in math and science.
This little hatchback **excels** in city traffic but feels weak on the highway.

drill.sentence: He was never a great student, but he really {{excelled}} at anything that involved building things with his hands.
drill.hint: was outstandingly good (one verb; not *shone* or *thrived*)

entries.related: *be good at* — the plain phrase; *shine* — do very well, often in one moment or area; *outperform* — do better than someone else.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To guide a conversation, a person or a process in a particular direction, often gently or without making it obvious.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in everyday talk: *steer the conversation toward* or *away from* a topic, *steer someone toward* a choice. It comes from steering a car or a boat and suggests quiet control. *Steer clear of* is a fixed phrase meaning *avoid*.
entries.pattern: steer + the conversation / someone + toward / away from + something; steer clear of
examples: Whenever someone mentioned the layoffs, the CEO **steered** the conversation back to sales.
The salesperson kept **steering** us toward the most expensive TV in the store.
Her high school counselor **steered** her away from art and toward engineering.

drill.sentence: When my aunt started asking about my love life, I quickly {{steered}} the conversation toward her garden.
drill.hint: took control of its direction, like a driver (not *turned*, *shifted*, *guided* or *redirected*)

entries.related: *steer clear of* — avoid; *guide* — plainer, usually helpful; *nudge* — push someone gently toward a choice.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The beginning of something, usually something unpleasant such as an illness or bad weather.
entries.usage: Common in medical and news language, almost always as *the onset of*: *the onset of symptoms*, *the onset of winter*. *Early-onset* describes a disease that starts younger than usual (*early-onset diabetes*). In casual speech people simply say *the start of*.
entries.pattern: the onset of + illness / symptoms / winter; early-onset + disease
examples: This medicine works best if you take it within 48 hours of the **onset** of symptoms.
With the **onset** of winter, the shelter opens every night instead of just on weekends.
He had **early-onset** arthritis, so he gave up running in his thirties.

drill.sentence: Many people feel sad and tired with the {{onset}} of the short, dark days in November.
drill.hint: the first stage of something unpleasant (not *start*, *arrival* or *beginning*)

mistake.wrong: I told them from the onset that I couldn't work weekends.
mistake.right: I told them from the outset that I couldn't work weekends.
mistake.why: *From the outset* means from the very beginning of any situation; *onset* is the start of something unpleasant.

entries.related: *outset* — the start of any activity (*from the outset*); *outbreak* — the sudden start of a disease or war; *start* — the plain word.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Happening or done too early, before the right or expected time.
entries.usage: Common in medicine (*a premature baby*, *premature death*) and in careful judgments: *It's premature to* + verb, *a premature decision*, *premature celebration*. *It would be premature to say* sounds careful and official; in casual speech people say *It's too early to say*. Both pree-muh-CHOOR and pree-muh-TOOR are normal in American English.
entries.pattern: premature + baby / birth / death / decision; it's premature to + verb
examples: Their twins were born six weeks **premature** and spent a month in the hospital.
It's **premature** to celebrate; we still have to win the last two games.
Analysts called the store closures **premature**, since sales were already recovering.

drill.sentence: The police said it would be {{premature}} to blame the driver before the investigation is finished.
drill.hint: done before the right time (one word; not *hasty* or *unfair*)

entries.related: *early* — neutral; *hasty* — done too quickly without enough thought; *overdue* — the opposite, later than expected.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person or thing that has the same role or position as another one, but in a different place, organization or system.
entries.usage: Very common in news and business: *the US president and his French counterpart*, *my counterpart at the other company*. It usually comes with a possessive (*her counterpart in Chicago*) or an adjective (*their male counterparts*, *its gas-powered counterpart*). It does not mean *opponent*.
entries.pattern: someone's counterpart (in / at + place); its (older / gas-powered) counterparts
examples: I'll be working closely with my **counterpart** in the Chicago office on this rollout.
The US secretary of state met her Japanese **counterpart** in Tokyo on Monday.
Electric cars still cost more than their gas-powered **counterparts**, but the gap is shrinking.

drill.sentence: Our school's principal called her {{counterpart}} at the rival school to plan a joint fundraiser.
drill.hint: the person with the same job there (not *colleague* or *equivalent*)

entries.related: *equivalent* — something equal in value or function; *colleague* — someone at your own workplace; *peer* — someone of the same rank or age.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To bring something back into use, activity or popularity after a period when it was weak or forgotten.
entries.usage: Common in news and culture: *revive a tradition*, *an old recipe*, *a TV show*, *the economy*, *interest in* something, *peace talks*. The noun is *revival* (*a revival of interest in vinyl*). It also means bring someone back to consciousness, as in first aid.
entries.pattern: revive + a tradition / interest / the economy / talks / a show
examples: The chef wants to **revive** forgotten Southern recipes from the 1800s.
Our neighborhood **revived** the tradition of a summer block party after a ten-year break.
Vinyl records have been **revived** by a new generation of music fans.

drill.sentence: The city wants to {{revive}} its empty downtown by turning old office buildings into apartments.
drill.hint: bring back to life and activity (not *revitalize*, *save* or *rebuild*)

entries.related: *revitalize* — give new energy to a place or an economy; *resurrect* — bring back something that seemed dead, stronger; *bring back* — the everyday phrase.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To survive pressure, force, an attack or hard conditions without being damaged or giving in.
entries.usage: Common in product descriptions, engineering and news: *withstand high temperatures*, *strong winds*, *pressure*, *criticism*, *close scrutiny*. It often follows *can*, *be able to* or *be built / designed to*. It is irregular like *stand*: *withstood*, *withstood*.
entries.pattern: withstand + heat / winds / pressure / criticism / scrutiny
examples: The windows are built to **withstand** winds of up to 150 miles per hour.
Their marriage has **withstood** two job losses and a move across the country.
Her argument couldn't **withstand** close scrutiny once people checked the numbers.

drill.sentence: These hiking boots can {{withstand}} freezing temperatures and deep snow without leaking.
drill.hint: formal verb: not be harmed by (not *handle*, *endure*, *survive* or *resist*)

mistake.wrong: The old barn withstanded the storm.
mistake.right: The old barn withstood the storm.
mistake.why: *Withstand* follows *stand*, so the past tense is *withstood*.

entries.related: *resist* — not be affected by (*water-resistant*); *endure* — suffer something difficult for a long time; *give way* — the opposite, break under pressure.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A situation or statement that seems impossible or self-contradictory because it combines two things that both seem true.
entries.usage: Common in serious conversation, journalism and essays: *It's a paradox that…*, *the paradox is that…*, *the paradox of* + noun. The adverb *paradoxically* often starts a sentence. Natives also say *ironic* for similar situations, but *paradox* stresses that two truths seem to clash.
entries.pattern: It's a paradox that …; the paradox of + noun; the paradox is that …
examples: It's a strange **paradox** that we have more ways to stay in touch than ever, yet so many people feel lonely.
Buying expensive boots to save money sounds like a **paradox**, but cheap ones fall apart in a year.
Psychologists call it the **paradox** of choice: with too many options, people end up less satisfied.

drill.sentence: It's a cruel {{paradox}} of insomnia that the harder you try to fall asleep, the more awake you feel.
drill.hint: two true things that seem to contradict each other (not *irony* or *contradiction*)

entries.related: *contradiction* — two things that cannot both be true; *irony* — a result that is the opposite of what you expected; *paradoxically* — the adverb.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: With every person in the group agreeing or voting the same way.
entries.usage: Common in news about votes and decisions: *vote*, *approve*, *agree* or *decide unanimously*, *be unanimously elected*. The adjective is *unanimous* (*a unanimous decision*). If even one person disagrees, it is not unanimous; for a very large majority, say *overwhelmingly*.
entries.pattern: vote / approve / agree / decide unanimously; be unanimously elected / approved
examples: The city council **unanimously** approved funding for a new public pool.
The judges **unanimously** chose her pie as the best at the county fair.
My roommates and I **unanimously** agreed that the old couch had to go.

drill.sentence: Every member of the school board voted yes, so the later start time was approved {{unanimously}}.
drill.hint: with everyone agreeing (not *easily*)

entries.related: *overwhelmingly* — by a very large majority, not everyone; *by consensus* — by general agreement, often without a vote; *split* — the opposite (*a split decision*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To succeed in reaching a goal, level or condition, usually after a lot of effort.
entries.usage: Formal; common in official, academic and business writing: *attain a goal*, *a level*, *a degree*, *a rank*, *financial independence*. In conversation natives say *reach*, *achieve* or *get*. It is rarely used for physical places; you *reach* a city or a summit.
entries.pattern: attain + a goal / a level / a degree / a rank / independence
examples: Fewer than one percent of students **attain** a perfect score on the exam.
She **attained** the rank of colonel before retiring from the Army.
For many young families, owning a home has become harder to **attain**.

drill.sentence: With steady training, he {{attained}} his goal of running a marathon in under four hours.
drill.hint: formal: succeeded in getting to (not *reached*, *achieved*, *met* or *hit*)

entries.related: *achieve* — the most common word for reaching a goal; *reach* — plainer, also for places and numbers; *attainable* — possible to reach.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: From time to time, often at fairly regular intervals.
entries.usage: Neutral and common in instructions, health advice and workplace writing: *check*, *review* or *update something periodically*. It is a little more formal than *every so often* or *now and then*, and it doesn't say exactly how often. It usually goes after the verb or before the main verb.
entries.pattern: check / review / update + something + periodically
examples: Stir the sauce **periodically** so it doesn't stick to the bottom of the pan.
The fitness app **periodically** reminds me to stand up and stretch.
A neighbor **periodically** checks on our house when we're out of town.

drill.sentence: It's a good idea to {{periodically}} check the air pressure in your tires, especially before a long drive.
drill.hint: every so often, at intervals (not *regularly* or *occasionally*)

entries.related: *regularly* — often and at a fixed rhythm; *occasionally* — sometimes, not often; *periodic* — the adjective (*periodic checkups*).

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Strong disagreement with an official or widely held opinion or decision.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, common in news, law and talk about organizations: *voice* or *express dissent*, *silence* or *crush dissent*, *dissent within the team*. A judge who disagrees with the majority writes *a dissent* (countable). It sounds the same as *descent* (going down), so check the spelling.
entries.pattern: voice / express dissent; silence / suppress dissent; write a dissent (judges)
examples: There was some **dissent** in the office when management ended the four-day workweek.
In a healthy team, **dissent** isn't punished; it's how bad ideas get caught early.
Two of the nine justices wrote a strong **dissent**, arguing that the law was too vague.

drill.sentence: The new club president doesn't tolerate {{dissent}}; anyone who questions her decisions gets kicked off the committee.
drill.hint: formal noun for refusing to agree with the official view (not *criticism*, *opposition* or *disagreement*)

entries.related: *disagreement* — plainer, any difference of opinion; *dissident* — a person who openly opposes a government; *consensus* — the opposite, general agreement.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Suddenly and without warning, often in a way that is surprising or a little rude.
entries.usage: Common in stories and news: *end*, *stop*, *leave* or *resign abruptly*, *hang up abruptly*. It often suggests that something was cut short or that the manner was rude. The adjective *abrupt* also describes a short, unfriendly way of speaking (*an abrupt reply*).
entries.pattern: end / stop / leave / resign / hang up abruptly
examples: Our video call ended **abruptly** when my laptop battery died in the middle of a sentence.
He **abruptly** hung up when I asked why the package was so late.
Halfway through dinner, my uncle stood up and left **abruptly**, without a word to anyone.

drill.sentence: The bus stopped so {{abruptly}} that everyone standing in the aisle almost fell over.
drill.hint: without any warning (not *suddenly*, *sharply* or *quickly*)

entries.related: *suddenly* — the plain word; *abrupt* — the adjective, also *rudely short* (*an abrupt reply*); *gradually* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Very strongly, or by a very large majority.
entries.usage: Common in news and reports about votes, surveys and reactions: *overwhelmingly positive* or *negative*, *vote overwhelmingly for* or *to*, and in descriptions of groups (*an overwhelmingly young audience*). It sounds factual, not emotional, unlike the adjective *overwhelming* for feelings. It means almost all, not all; for everyone, say *unanimously*.
entries.pattern: overwhelmingly + positive / negative / young; vote overwhelmingly for / to
examples: Reviews of the new restaurant have been **overwhelmingly** positive, so it's booked for weeks.
Residents voted **overwhelmingly** to build a new skate park by the river.
The crowd at the comic convention was **overwhelmingly** young, mostly teenagers and college students.

drill.sentence: In the survey, hotel guests {{overwhelmingly}} preferred the new breakfast menu: 92 percent chose it over the old one.
drill.hint: by a very large majority (not *clearly*, *strongly*, *largely* or *mostly*)

entries.related: *unanimously* — with everyone agreeing; *largely* — mostly, weaker; *overwhelming* — the adjective (*an overwhelming majority*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To give a lot of your time, energy, money or attention to a particular activity, person or purpose.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *devote time / energy / resources to* something, *devote yourself to*, *be devoted to* someone (love and care for them deeply). Here *to* is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form. *Dedicate* is very close and a little more formal.
entries.pattern: devote + time / energy / money + to + noun / -ing; devote yourself to; be devoted to + person
examples: She **devoted** most of her twenties to building her own furniture company.
The local newspaper **devoted** its entire front page to the flood.
He's completely **devoted** to his kids and rarely misses a soccer game.

drill.sentence: After he retired, he {{devoted}} his weekends to restoring old pinball machines.
drill.hint: put a lot of time and energy into this (not *dedicated*, *gave* or *committed*)

mistake.wrong: I want to devote more time to learn the piano.
mistake.right: I want to devote more time to learning the piano.
mistake.why: In *devote … to*, *to* is a preposition, so a verb after it takes the *-ing* form.

entries.related: *dedicate* — very similar, a bit more formal, also *dedicate a book to someone*; *be devoted to* — love and support someone deeply; *spend time on* — the neutral phrase.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To grow well and be healthy, or to develop successfully and do very well.
entries.usage: Used for plants, businesses, people, communities and the arts: *Lavender flourishes in dry soil*, *The business flourished*. It has no object. It sounds a little more literary than *thrive*, which is the closest synonym and more common in casual speech.
entries.pattern: plants / businesses / people / the arts + flourish
examples: Lavender **flourishes** in dry, sunny spots and needs almost no water.
Small bookstores are **flourishing** again in some cities, despite online competition.
Some kids struggle in big classes but **flourish** with a little individual attention.

drill.sentence: With cheap rent and lots of young artists, the neighborhood's music scene {{flourished}} in the 1990s.
drill.hint: grew strong and successful (not *thrived*, *boomed* or *blossomed*)

entries.related: *thrive* — very similar, more common in speech; *blossom* — develop and become more attractive or successful; *wither* — the opposite, slowly weaken or die.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Only average in quality; not very good, though not terrible.
entries.usage: Always critical, and common in conversation and reviews of food, movies, work and performance: *mediocre at best*, *a mediocre student*. It sounds harsher than *okay* or *average*, because it implies that more was expected. The stress is on the third syllable: mee-dee-OH-ker.
entries.pattern: mediocre + food / results / performance; mediocre at best
examples: The hotel was beautiful, but the restaurant downstairs was **mediocre**, so we ate out every night.
He was a **mediocre** student in high school and became a brilliant engineer later on.
After two **mediocre** seasons, the team finally made the playoffs.

drill.sentence: Everyone raved about that new taco place, but honestly, the food was {{mediocre}} at best: dry tortillas and bland salsa.
drill.hint: only average, a letdown (not *average*, *okay*, *so-so* or *decent*)

entries.related: *average* — neutral, not critical; *so-so* and *meh* — informal, about the same; *second-rate* — clearly below standard.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A state of great confusion, uncertainty and disorder, in a country, an organization, a market or a person's mind.
entries.usage: Common in news and in talk about personal crises: *political*, *economic* or *emotional turmoil*, *be in turmoil*, *throw something into turmoil*, *a period of turmoil*. It is uncountable, so *a turmoil* is rare. It is a bit more formal than *chaos* and often describes a longer period.
entries.pattern: in turmoil; throw / plunge something into turmoil; political / emotional / financial turmoil
examples: The founder's surprise resignation threw the company into **turmoil**.
After her parents' divorce, she was in emotional **turmoil** for most of a year.
Stock markets around the world fell sharply during the financial **turmoil** of 2008.

drill.sentence: When the airline's booking system crashed, the airport was in complete {{turmoil}}, with thousands of travelers stuck.
drill.hint: a state of great disorder (not *chaos*, *confusion* or *disarray*)

entries.related: *chaos* — complete disorder, stronger and more physical; *upheaval* — a big, sudden change; *stability* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Never stopping or getting weaker, often in a way that is tiring, harsh or impressive.
entries.usage: It can be negative (*relentless rain*, *heat*, *pressure*, *criticism*) or admiring (*a relentless worker*, *relentless focus*). Common in weather reports, news, sports and business praise. The adverb *relentlessly* is also common (*relentlessly cheerful*).
entries.pattern: relentless + pressure / heat / rain / criticism / pace; be relentless in + -ing
examples: The **relentless** heat that summer made it impossible to sleep without a fan.
She's **relentless** when she wants something; she called the store every day until they found her order.
The **relentless** pace of the job burned out three managers in two years.

drill.sentence: Our new puppy is {{relentless}}: she drops her ball at my feet every five minutes until I throw it.
drill.hint: never letting up, to the point of wearing you out (not *persistent*, *tireless*, *determined* or *exhausting*)

entries.related: *persistent* — keeps going, with a neutral tone; *unrelenting* — same meaning, more formal; *tireless* — always positive, hardworking.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To happen at the same time as something else.
entries.usage: Common in news, planning and schedules: *coincide with* + event, *(be) timed to coincide with*. It is used for events and periods, not people. Unlike the noun *coincidence*, the verb does not suggest chance: a launch can be *timed to coincide with* a holiday on purpose.
entries.pattern: coincide with + event; (be) timed to coincide with
examples: This year my birthday **coincides** with Thanksgiving, so we're having one big dinner.
The album's release was timed to **coincide** with the band's world tour.
The rise in break-ins **coincided** with the closing of the neighborhood police station.

drill.sentence: Our trip to Rio happened to {{coincide}} with Carnival, so every hotel in the city was booked.
drill.hint: take place at the same time (not *overlap* or *clash*)

entries.related: *overlap* — partly happen at the same time; *clash with* — happen at the same time in an inconvenient way; *coincidence* — a surprising chance event.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Hard to find, catch, achieve, remember or define.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and writing about goals, animals and ideas: *an elusive goal*, *title* or *cure*, *an elusive animal*. It often follows *remain* or *prove*: *A solution remains elusive*, *Sleep proved elusive*. It is neutral, with a slightly literary feel.
entries.pattern: remain / prove elusive; an elusive + goal / animal / cure / title
examples: Snow leopards are so **elusive** that people spend years in the mountains without seeing one.
A first championship has proved **elusive** for the city's baseball team.
Sleep was **elusive** the night before my driving test.

drill.sentence: After hours of searching, the cause of the leak in our roof remained {{elusive}}.
drill.hint: hard to find (not *unclear*, *unknown* or *a mystery*)

entries.related: *evasive* — avoiding direct answers on purpose, about people; *slippery* — informal, hard to hold or pin down; *within reach* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Lasting longer than expected or wanted, often while slowly fading.
entries.usage: Typical with *doubts*, *concerns*, *questions*, *effects*, *symptoms*, *a cough* or *a smell*: *lingering doubts*, *a lingering cough*. It is neutral and common in news and everyday talk. The verb is *linger* (*The smell lingered for days*).
entries.pattern: lingering + doubts / concerns / effects / cough / smell
examples: I've had a **lingering** cough ever since I had the flu in March.
Even after the inspection, the buyers had **lingering** doubts about the roof.
The **lingering** smell of last night's fish was still in the kitchen when we came down for breakfast.

drill.sentence: The economy is growing again, but the {{lingering}} effects of the recession are still felt in many small towns.
drill.hint: not yet gone, slow to fade (not *lasting*, *remaining*, *ongoing* or *long-term*)

entries.related: *persistent* — continuing, often stubbornly; *lasting* — long-term or permanent, often positive (*a lasting friendship*); *fleeting* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A fixed and oversimplified idea about what a type of person or thing is like, often unfair or untrue.
entries.usage: Common in news, education and conversation: *a stereotype about* or *of* a group, *the stereotype that…*, *fit*, *break*, *challenge* or *reinforce a stereotype*. It is also a verb (*be stereotyped as*), and the adjective *stereotypical* is common. It is usually critical of the idea, not the group.
entries.pattern: a stereotype about / of + group; the stereotype that …; fit / break / challenge / reinforce a stereotype
examples: There's a **stereotype** that Germans have no sense of humor, but my coworker from Berlin is hilarious.
He loves ballet and can't stand country music, which doesn't fit the **stereotype** of a Texas rancher.
The show makes fun of old **stereotypes** about shy, nerdy scientists.

drill.sentence: My aunt is a librarian who rides a motorcycle and plays in a punk band; she breaks every {{stereotype}}.
drill.hint: fixed, oversimplified idea about a type of person (not *cliché* or *rule*)

entries.related: *cliché* — an overused phrase or idea; *prejudice* — an unfair dislike based on such ideas; *stereotypical* — the adjective.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Slow to act, speak or decide because you are unsure, nervous or worried.
entries.usage: Common at work, in news and in conversation: *hesitant to* + verb, *hesitant about* + noun or *-ing*, *a hesitant smile*. It is softer and more polite than *unwilling*: *I'm a bit hesitant to commit* signals doubt without saying no. The verb is *hesitate*.
entries.pattern: hesitant to + verb; hesitant about + noun / -ing
examples: Many small businesses are **hesitant** to hire until they know where the economy is headed.
I was **hesitant** about moving to a new city, but it turned out to be the best decision I've made.
She gave a **hesitant** smile and finally raised her hand.

drill.sentence: I'm a little {{hesitant}} to lend him my car again after what happened to the bumper.
drill.hint: unsure and slow to do it (not *reluctant*, *unwilling* or *nervous*)

entries.related: *reluctant* — not wanting to do something; *wary* — careful because of possible danger; *eager* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Having a good reputation, so that people trust its quality or honesty.
entries.usage: Used for businesses, sources and professionals: *a reputable dealer*, *company*, *contractor*, *breeder* or *news source*. It is very common in advice (*Buy from a reputable seller*). The stress is on the first syllable; the opposite is *disreputable*.
entries.pattern: a reputable + dealer / company / source / contractor / breeder
examples: Before you get a tattoo, make sure the studio is **reputable** and uses sterile equipment.
For health questions, stick to **reputable** websites, like the ones run by major hospitals.
We found a **reputable** contractor through friends, and the kitchen was finished on time.

drill.sentence: If you want a puppy, go to a {{reputable}} breeder or a shelter, not a pet store with no history.
drill.hint: known to be honest and trustworthy (not *trusted*, *respected* or *reliable*)

mistake.why: Learners stress it like *repute*, but the stress falls on the first syllable.

entries.related: *reliable* — can be depended on to work or be correct; *respectable* — socially acceptable, decent; *disreputable* — the opposite.
